power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Purpose: Visual acuity (VA) testing has expanded from examiner-guided to examinee self-guided assessments, yet measurement variability may limit clinical utility.
This meta-analysis investigated VA-tests' intertest and test-retest accuracy and precision across different testing strategies.
Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus for VA validation studies published between 1 January 1983 to 02 December 2024.
Eligible studies reported intertest or test-retest Bland-Altman mean bias and limits of agreement (LoA); objective VA assessments and correlation coefficient only studies were excluded.
Testing strategies were classified by test site, optotype sampling methods, response input methods, and level of supervision.
Accuracy outcomes were reported as mean biases.
Precision outcomes were reported as intertest LoA half-width and test-retest coefficient of repeatability (CoR) for test-retest.
Multilevel random-effects models accounted for multiple estimates per study.
Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2.
Results: Across 82 included studies (10,873 participants), pooled intertest and testretest mean biases were both 0.01 logMAR.
Intertest LoA half-width was 0.19 logMAR and test-retest CoR was 0.14 logMAR.

Variability showed marginal difference by optotype sampling (adaptive: LoA half-width 0.20 logMAR, CoR 0.15 logMAR; fixed: 0.18, 0.13) or response input method (examiner: 0.19, 0.13; self-run: 0.19, 0.18).

Only few studies reported results for test site and level of supervision, hence only intertest was compared (test site, clinic: LoA half-width 0.19 logMAR vs remote 0.27 logMAR and level of supervision, supervised: 0.19 logMAR vs unsupervised 0.26 logMAR).
QUADAS-2 identified patient selection as the domain of greatest bias concern.
Conclusion: Across testing strategies, VA assessments showed minimal systematic bias but substantial variability.
Lack of precision is more notable in remote and unsupervised testing while no difference within optotype sampling and response-input methods.
Future development should prioritize on improving precision of visual acuity tests with finer adaptive optotype resolution and remote/unsupervised testings through repeatability studies.
Globally, 2.2 billion people have visual impairment, with a substantial impact on development and quality of life (1).
text.formatted: Globally, 2.2 billion people have visual impairment, with a substantial impact on development and quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Visual acuity (VA) is the primary measure of vision in ophthalmology and optometry (2, 3), underpinning disease monitoring, treatment evaluation, and clinical trial endpoints (4).
text.formatted: Visual acuity (VA) is the primary measure of vision in ophthalmology and optometry <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref>, underpinning disease monitoring, treatment evaluation, and clinical trial endpoints <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: The Earyl Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart is widely used as a reference standard in rigorous clinical research (5).
text.formatted: The Earyl Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) chart is widely used as a reference standard in rigorous clinical research <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: However, routine VA testing remains heterogenous, ranging from conventional charts, such as Snellen and LEA charts, to examiner-guided and selfadministered adaptive digital tests.
Software and mobile platforms(6-10) have further extended testing beyond traditional clinical settings, including patient's homes and emergency departments (11) (12) (13).
text.formatted: Software and mobile platforms(6-10) have further extended testing beyond traditional clinical settings, including patient's homes and emergency departments <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: This diversity in chart design, administration, testing environment, and patient characteristics raises a fundamental question: do these approaches yield VA measurements that are reproducible and comparable?
VA is the primary outcome measure in optometric and ophthalmic clinical care and science.
Various ways to measure it have been established since its earliest application (14).
text.formatted: Various ways to measure it have been established since its earliest application <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref>.

text.text: Conventionally, VA is measured at a dedicated eyecare facility using a wall-mounted or retro-illuminated chart 6 meters from the observer to reduce the influence of near-accommodation and pupil constriction reflex.
The administrator then proctors the exam and scores the performance as smallest legible line as logMAR, decimal, or Snellen notation (5).
text.formatted: The administrator then proctors the exam and scores the performance as smallest legible line as logMAR, decimal, or Snellen notation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Modifications in psychophysical procedures, optotypes, viewing distances, and administration strategies permit VA tests to be performed within a clinical environment, or remotely, without administrator's proctoring and scoring (8, 10) This expansion in where VA is measured has been matched by variation in how, namely the psychophysical procedure and scoring convention.
text.formatted: Modifications in psychophysical procedures, optotypes, viewing distances, and administration strategies permit VA tests to be performed within a clinical environment, or remotely, without administrator's proctoring and scoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10)</ref> This expansion in where VA is measured has been matched by variation in how, namely the psychophysical procedure and scoring convention.

text.text: Fixed presentation shows every optotype on every line and has fixed size change steps between line of optotypes, e.g., ETDRS 0.10 logMAR.
Adaptive procedures instead select each subsequent optotype based on prior response using staircase procedures, Bayesian algorithms, or adaptive charts (10, 15).
text.formatted: Adaptive procedures instead select each subsequent optotype based on prior response using staircase procedures, Bayesian algorithms, or adaptive charts <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15)</ref>.

text.text: These tests enable estimations of threshold in a customized way and may have finer test resolution (i.e. smaller step sizes between rendered stimuli (10, 16)) compared to ETDRS's 0.10 logMAR step size.
text.formatted: These tests enable estimations of threshold in a customized way and may have finer test resolution (i.e. smaller step sizes between rendered stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16)</ref>) compared to ETDRS's 0.10 logMAR step size.

text.text: Moreover, these tests may provide additional information about the psychophysical performance compared to chart-based tasks (e.g., slope of psychometric function) (17).
text.formatted: Moreover, these tests may provide additional information about the psychophysical performance compared to chart-based tasks (e.g., slope of psychometric function) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: Routinely VA is measured in a dedicated eye-care facility where the testing environment is usually held constant.

Testing distance is determined by the room set-up (e.g., fixed distance between the examination chair and eye chart) with ambient illumination and chart luminance maintained within recommend ranges per ISO 8596 guidelines (18) or ETDRS protocol (5, 19).
text.formatted: Testing distance is determined by the room set-up (e.g., fixed distance between the examination chair and eye chart) with ambient illumination and chart luminance maintained within recommend ranges per ISO 8596 guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18)</ref> or ETDRS protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, glare and visual distractions were usually minimized.

Since these conditions are unlikely to change within the same clinic, patients who consistently return to the same clinic for follow-up visits are less subjected to variability introduced by the different environments.
However, if test were performed on different clinical sites, variation in any of these settings could contribute to measurement variability.
However, not all VA assessments were performed in an eye-clinic.
For example, patients in the emergency department with visual concerns will need to be evaluated for visual acuity.
In the United States, passing a driver's license test also require checking of VA at the business office, instead of a dedicate eye clinic.
During COVID-19, a surge in development of remote VA testing further allows at-home testing (20, 21).
text.formatted: During COVID-19, a surge in development of remote VA testing further allows at-home testing <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: Unlike eye clinics, these testing environments are less consistent.
Viewing distance can be established with facial recognition apps (7).
text.formatted: Viewing distance can be established with facial recognition apps <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Viewing angle, ambient lighting, and screen glare also varies.
Screen size, resolution, brightness, and calibration may also vary across devices.
In visual acuity tests, optotype sampling determines how subsequent optotypes are selected.
Fixed sampling refers to predetermined sequences of optotypes e.g., letter sequence in ETDRS across lines.
In adaptive sampling methods, sequences of letters or orientations of optotypes are randomized, thereby eliminating memorization bias.

Different optotypes used to test patients may require demographic (e.g., symbols for young children) and regional (e.g., charts using letters in Roman and in Arabic letters), hence inducing another source of variability due to their differences in meaning, physical spatial contents.
Orientation judgement paradigms using Landolt C or tumbling E optotypes avoid these intertest confounders as only optotype size and gap orientation is varied.
In the context of intertest comparison, letter identification and orientation judgments undergo different neural computations, thus adding additional variability.
Secondly, adaptive sampling uses various algorithm to select the next stimulus or set of stimuli based on previous responses.
Additionally, some adaptive tasks do not have a fixed step size between varying optotype sizes, which allows finer resolution of acuity tests (6, 7, 10, 22, 23).
text.formatted: Additionally, some adaptive tasks do not have a fixed step size between varying optotype sizes, which allows finer resolution of acuity tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23)</ref>.

text.text: The current gold-standard logMAR chart, such as ETDRS, includes 5-same sized-stimuli per line scaled at 0.10logMAR step size at a given distance using a 10 alternative forced choice task (24).
text.formatted: The current gold-standard logMAR chart, such as ETDRS, includes 5-same sized-stimuli per line scaled at 0.10logMAR step size at a given distance using a 10 alternative forced choice task <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: The scoring is recommended such that all letters need to be identified correctly to receive the score, or stop at the line if this criterion is not met (24).
text.formatted: The scoring is recommended such that all letters need to be identified correctly to receive the score, or stop at the line if this criterion is not met <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Threshold or visual acuity is then determined as the last line that had no errors.
However, some users may deploy a more lenient criterion, such as identifying 3 or 4 letters correctly before accepting the line, to account for various sources of noise (25).
text.formatted: However, some users may deploy a more lenient criterion, such as identifying 3 or 4 letters correctly before accepting the line, to account for various sources of noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: Scoring by letter-counting is another method (0.02 logMAR per correct letter) often applied.
However, it discounts that the letter size within each line is the same.
Additionally, it also dismissed the effect of a 60% correct criterion measures at a different point of the psychometric function than at 100% correct.
Hence, these scoring methods are misleading and contributing to variance in VA measurements.
The method by which an examinee's responses are recorded is another source of variability.

In conventional testings with letter-based charts (e.g., ETDRS, Snellen, and Bailey-Lovie) or symbol-based charts (e.g., LEA symbols), the examinee typically name each optotype out loud and the examiner judges whether the response is correct in order to continue to the next line or terminate the test.
For orientation-based optotypes (e.g., Landolt C or Tumbling E), responses may be given verbally or by gesture.
In each case, the examiner records the response manually or enters it into a computer system.
An examiner's judgement on scoring and error in calculation could introduce variability in VA measurements.
Alternatively, some VA assessments that enable examinee to enter their own responses using methods such as touchscreens (6, 10, 22, 26), keyboards (16, 23, 27, 28), or voice recognition (29).

text.text: Each method has its own potential sources of error and may therefore affect the accuracy and precision of measurements in different ways.
Whether a VA assessment is supervised or not could be another variable that impact measurement accuracy and precision.
In routine clinical testing, a trained technician is present in the room and administers the test.
Their role may include providing instructions, ensuring consistent viewing distance, and scoring the results.
The degree of examiner involvement, however, based on design of the assessment.
Some tests heavily rely on the examiner, who is responsible for response input, optotype selection, and scoring.
Others, such as automated tests with examinee self-input, require minimal involvement, and the examiner only serve to oversee the test and provide technical assistance as needed.
Regardless of how involved the examiner is, it remains important to determine whether supervision is associated with accuracy and precision of VA testings.
Viewing distance is a further source of variation.

The standard 6-meter (20 feet) distance approximates optical infinity, minimizing accommodation's and pupil constriction's contributions to threshold(5) whereas near-and intermediate VAs are typically measured at 40cm (16 in) and 67cm (26 in), respectively (30) (31) (32).

text.text: Like procedure and scoring, distance is often confounded with modality, since remote and mobile tests skew toward shorter distances.
Validation of VA tests is commonly established by repeatability and intertest agreement experiments.
A repeatability experiment consists of comparison two-measurements of the same test.
For intertest agreement experiment, a reference test is compared against a newly developed test to estimate its agreement.
Note that during such experiment, no ground truth exists.
Nevertheless, the comparison between two-tests has clinical utility in determining whether tests results are interchangeable.

Consequently, without clear estimates of a VA-test's repeatability and intertest-agreement, an interpretation of results within and between tests remains challenging and prevents meaningful judgement during clinical trials and in clinical practices.
Agreement and repeatability can be evaluated using several statistical approaches, each with distinct limitations.

The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) measures relative reliability but is influenced by between-participants variability and does not directly show the magnitude or direction of paired differences (38).

text.text: The coefficient of variation (CoV), which expresses variability relative to the mean, does not directly assess paired agreement and can be difficult to interpret when logMAR values approach or cross zero.

Bland-Altman analysis instead characterized paired differences using the mean bias and 95% limits of agreement (LoA) (39) (40) (41) Van der Zee et al. investigated broader range of VA tests and reported the overall mean systematic bias of 0.03 logMAR and overall mean 95%LoA of ±0.20 logMAR in distance VA measured in adults (44).

text.text: However, these previous reviews focused on digital and self-administered VA test in adults and did not separately characterize intertest and testretest outcomes across testing characteristics.

The current study's primary objective was therefore to evaluate the precision and accuracy of a visual acuity test's repeatability and intertest agreement along four factors of variability: (1) test sites (clinic vs remote), (2) optotype sampling (fixed vs adaptive), (3) response input method (examiner vs self), and (4) level of supervision (supervised vs unsupervised).
We hypothesized that VA tests precision will decreases with added sources of test variability.
Moreover, based on prior meta-analyses (42, 44), we hypothesized that accuracy outcomes are not significantly affected by increased sources of variability.

text.text: The test site described where VA was assessed.
Testing in a dedicated research or eye care facility was classified as "clinic," whereas testing elsewhere, such as home, was classified as "remote."
Next, "Optotype sampling" describes how optotype sizes were generated and displayed.
Since the optotype size sampling dictates what the actual optotype sizes in any given test are, it determines a VA task's resolution.
For example, VA tests with 0.10 logMAR size change per line on the ETDRS chart have a resolution of 0.10 logMAR and thus cannot measure any smaller changes.
Tests using "fixed sampling" presented sizes in a predetermined sequence and terminated according to a pre-specified stopping rule, such as maximum number of errors at a given size.
Examples included retro-illuminated ETDRS charts, Rosenbaum near acuity card, and digital charts with fixed increments (54) (55) (56) (57) .

Three-level random-effects metaregression models were fitted using the metafor package.
These models accounted for multiple effect estimates from the same study and distinguished sampling error, variation among effects within studies, and variation between studies.
Effect estimates, k, refer to data points in the meta-regression contributed by a study.
For example, a study evaluating 2 different index VA tests across the same population will be contributing to 2 effect estimates.
The within-study and between-study variation was estimated using restricted maximum likelihood (REML).
An overall pooled estimate and 95% CI were calculated for each outcome.
For each outcome, separate three-level meta-regression models were fitted for test sites, psychophysical procedure, response input, and supervision.
An additional model compared the observed combination of these four testing strategies as distinct testing groups.
Differences between testing groups were evaluated using study-clustered CR2 robust Wald tests with the HTZ small-sample adjustment using the clubSandwish package.
When the test could not be calculated, the model-based moderator test was reported and identified as such.

text.text: Prior investigations have proposed benchmarks for interpreting variability in VA measurements.
Siderov and Tiu suggested that a difference of at least 0.15 logMAR was needed to confidently identify a real change under routine clinical conditions(112).
In this meta-analysis, systematic accuracy and precisions of validated visual acuity assessments were quantified across testing strategies and participants' characteristics.

The overall index VA tests demonstrated pooled systematic intertest mean bias very close to 0.00 logMAR, indicating the VA measured with index tests provided very similar results as the reference test.

However, with the pooled systematic LoA half-width of 0.19 logMAR, it indicates we are expected to see variation of 0.19 logMAR (approximately 2 ETDRS lines) when comparing results from different tests.

When different charts are used at follow-up visits, a change of less than 0.19 logMAR may clinically indicate a change in vision, but mathematically, may be difficult to distinguish from the expected variability between the tests.

When dissecting into different testing strategies, we observed a statistically significantly wider (p=0.030) intertest LoA half-width between VA conducted in non-clinical test site ("remote") and those conducted in a controlled clinical test site ("clinic").
This observation was also present when comparing intertest precision across different combination of testing strategies.

Though the comparisons did not reach a statistically significant threshold when evaluating testing strategies among different combinations, there was a trend toward greater variability (LoA half-width 0.27 and 0.25 logMAR, Figure 5) in testing strategies involving remote testings.
text.formatted: Though the comparisons did not reach a statistically significant threshold when evaluating testing strategies among different combinations, there was a trend toward greater variability (LoA half-width 0.27 and 0.25 logMAR, Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>) in testing strategies involving remote testings.

text.text: One consideration for the observed difference in variability was the imbalance of sample size.

The remote subgroup included only 6 studies and 8 effect estimates, compared with 61 studies and 99 effect estimates in the clinic subgroup, making the remote pooled estimate more sensitive to individual studies.

Another aspect to consider was that remote testings often coincided with unsupervised and examinee self-inputted responses, making the contribution of these characteristics difficult to differentiate.

However, on the paired-wise comparison within each testing strategy, LoA half-width did not differ significantly by input method (examiner vs self; p=0.925) and level of supervision (supervised vs unsupervised; p=0.108).
One "Remote / Adaptive / Examiner / Supervised" combination had a LoA half-width of 0.48 logMAR, which is more than twice of the overall pooled value of 0.19 logMAR.
This combination was omitted from the combination level analysis was it was represented by a single effect estimate (8).
text.formatted: This combination was omitted from the combination level analysis was it was represented by a single effect estimate <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: However, it could still contribute to the variability in overall pooled LoA half-width in the "remote" subgroup.
Regardless, it highlights the substantial variability in remote testing can still occur even when conducted with the examiner input and under supervision.
In intertest agreement, testing conditions with increase sources of variability were associated with widen LoA half-width across VA tests, while differences in bias were marginal.

These findings suggest that precision is more susceptible than accuracy to potential sources of variability in VA testing strategies and highlight that VA measurements can be accurate on average yet imprecise at the individual level.
We also observed a similar result pattern for test-retest comparisons.
The pooled systematic test-retest mean bias was very close to 0.00 logMAR, indicating no overall learning or fatigue effects that would yield a better or worse results upon repeated testing.
However, the lack of precision was evident.

The systematic pooled test-retest CoR of 0.14 logMAR indicates if the same test were to be repeated, a difference that's smaller than 0.14 logMAR would be mathematically considered as the measurement variability within the test, not a true meaningful change.

While the solution for intertest variability would be addressed by using the same eye chart and testing strategies when following up with patients, the lack of precision in test-retest poses a greater limitation in advancing assessments with wide test-retest CoR for clinical use, especially when monitoring change in subtle VA is crucial in evaluating treatment outcome and influencing clinical decision making.
In evaluation of test-retest CoR within each testing strategies, we found a significant difference in CoR between tests that utilized examiner-input versus examinee self-input (p=0.030).
The CoR for self-inputted tests to be wider than those of examiner-inputted (0.18 vs 0.13 logMAR; p=0.030), but the difference of 0.05 logMAR may not be clinically significant.
The increased variability in self-inputted tests could be explained by the differences in how examinee self-inputted their responses.
Some utilized keypads labeled with corresponding orientation of the optotype (23, 27, 28) or corresponding Kay Pictures (16) .

text.text: In addition to the methodology of how the responses were recorded, another variable worth mentioning is whether different psychophysical procedures could influence the variability observed in self-inputted VA tests.
In fixed procedure, the scoring rules were line-by-line or letter-by-letter with relatively coarse increment.
In adaptive procedure, optotype sizes were adjusted based on preceding responses and enable finer increments of VA measurement.
Finer scoring in adaptive procedure may capture smaller differences in response that would be rounded to the same acuity value with line-based scoring.
Thus, increasing the observed measurement variability.
This is consistent with the findings in our analysis, where adaptive psychophysical procedure has wider CoR than fixed, but the differences did not reach a significant level.
Regardless, within self-inputted VA tests, 13 studies utilized adaptive and 2 studies utilized fixed psychophysical procedure.
The predominant representation of adaptive procedure in self-inputted test may contribute to the variability in self-inputted VA tests.
In evaluation of CoR among different combination of testing strategies, we observed similar pattern as described above.

Test-retest CoR was the least precise in the combination that included adaptive procedure and examinee self-inputted testing (CoR 0.19 logMAR) compared to those of fixed procedures and examiner-inputted testings (CoR 0.13 and 0.14 logMAR), though again, the differences were not significant.
Overall, we observed decrease in precision in testings that involved adaptive psychophysical procedure and examinee self-inputted testing strategies.
Of the 38 studies that involved adaptive sampling, majority of the studies (n=32) relied on ETDRS as prototype of their chart design, which confined their step-size resolution to 0.10 logMAR.
Similarly, most testing with fixed procedure (i.e., either fixed chartbased or fixed adaptive tests) followed the design of the ETDRS chart.

Furthermore, some adaptive sampling methods may have additional free parameters (e.g. slope, lapse rate, differing Bayesian prior settings, etc.) and thus have more degree of freedom for test variability.
Consequently, future studies should investigate the relationship between test resolution and different of parameters in adaptive protocol.
Beyond testing strategies, we also evaluated accuracy and precision on who were tested on the VA tests.
Previous work (44) excluded individuals younger than 18 years, in part because the use of age-appropriate charts and optotypes were expected to introduce additional heterogeneity.

text.text: Most included studies involving children used charts or optotypes also commonly used in adults, including ETDRS, Snellen, or Landolt C.
One study used Baile-Lovie acuity chart (76), and another study used Kay Pictures (75).

text.text: In our meta-analysis, we found a statistically significant difference in intertest accuracy (mean bias) of VA measured between adults and children (0.02 vs -0.04 logMAR; p=0.008).
The negative mean bias indicates that index tests yielded lower logMAR values, corresponding to better VA, than reference tests.
In another word, index tests measured better VA than references tests by 0.04 logMAR in children and worse VA than references by 0.02 logMAR in adults.

Although intertest mean bias differed significantly between children and adults, the absolute between-group difference was small at 0.06 logMAR, suggesting the difference may have limited clinical relevance.
No significant difference between children and adults were detected in intertest precision, test-retest accuracy, or test-retest precision.
In both age groups, LoA-half width and CoR estimates were similar to the systematic pooled estimates.
These findings provide no clear evidence that pediatric inclusion or use of age-appropriate testing reduced VA agreement or repeatability.
The presence of ocular pathologies may also influence accuracy and precision of VA measurements.
Amblyopia and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) were the most represented conditions in this dataset.
These conditions could theoretically affect performance through unstable fixation, impaired contrast perception, or fluctuating visual function (114).
text.formatted: These conditions could theoretically affect performance through unstable fixation, impaired contrast perception, or fluctuating visual function <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">(114)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, test-retest CoR did not differ significantly between those without versus those with ocular pathologies (0.14 vs 0.13 logMAR; p=0.387).
Similarly, there was no significant difference in intertest LoA half-widths between either pathology subgroups (0.17 logMAR in without vs 0.18 logMAR in with pathology; p=0.467).
Intertest and test-retest accuracies were both around 0.00 logMAR (Supplementary Material, Figure S7).

text.text: In our meta-analysis, differences in accuracy and precision between age groups and ocular health status were generally small.
However, these analyses are limited to broad comparisons and limit the generalizability of our findings to specific age ranges, ocular diagnosis, or level of disease severity.
Several limitations should be considered.

First, the imbalance in number of studies and effect estimates across testing strategies may have reduced the precision of subgroup comparisons and made sparely represented categories more sensitive to individual studies.
Studies also contributed different number of effect estimates with varying sample size and sampling variance, resulting in unequal contribution to the pooled estimates.
Although our multilevel models and cluster-robust inference accounted for dependence among effect estimates from the same study, uneven representation across testing strategies remains a limitation.
This limitation was evident in the testretest analysis.

Several VA assessments, including Odysight(103), DigiVis(21), and myVisionTrack(110), have been developed for home self-testing or remote monitoring between clinic visits, but remote and unsupervised testing were each represented by only one study in our test-retest analysis.
This limits our conclusions about repeatability under these intended conditions and highlight the need for further validation for longitudinal monitoring.
Secondly, the methodological quality and clinical applicability of included studies was variable.

Common patient-selection concerns included convenience or nonconsecutive recruitment, and many validation studies predominantly enrolled healthy young patients, limiting their applicability to boarder range of patient and ocular conditions encountered in clinical practice.

Additionally, studies often did not clearly report whether examiners were masked to the results of the alternative test, which could influence test scoring, interpretation and potentially overestimate the agreement.

These findings, together with substantial heterogeneity in intertest and testretest estimates, highlight the need for rigorously designed validation studies using representative clinical population, prespecified testing protocols and masked assessment when feasible.
Thirdly, we did not evaluate whether optotype design or the specific pairing of index and reference tests influence intertest agreement.

Although ETDRS-based testing is widely regarded as the standardized reference for VA in clinical research(115), it was used as the comparator in only a little over half of the included intertest studies.
Snellen, Landolt C, and Tumbling E charts were among other commonly used reference tests.
The difference in optotype design, chart layout, crowding, scoring rules, and test-termination criteria may affect both systematic differences and the spread of differences between tests.
Importantly, intertest LoA reflects the combined variability of the index and reference tests.
Therefore, LoA halfwidth cannot be attributed solely to the performance of the index test.

Consequently, heterogeneity in reference test selection may have contributed to the observed intertest variability in LoA half-width and potentially confounded comparisons across testing methodologies.

text.text: We found that optotype sampling and response input method do not affect VA test 790 precision but that testing site and level of supervision associated with great variability.
The lack of difference in precision between fixed and adaptive sampling was likely due 792 to use of fixed resolution of 0.10logMAR.
This limits detection of finer resolution and 793 constrained the smallest detectable change to 0.10logMAR.
Likewise, a change would 794 need to exceed 2 ETDRS lines to be considered a meaningful change beyond 795 measurement noise.
While ETDRS has been regarded as the gold-standard of VA 796 measurement in the past decades, it may not be as sensitive to small changes in VA.

797 While the addition of variability through different testing strategies, such as remote and 798 unsupervised testings, add another layer of heterogeneity to VA assessments, contributing to the poor intertest agreement (0.19logMAR) and test-retest repeatability (0.14 logMAR).
These findings suggest future development of VA assessment should aim to develop adaptive optotype sampling with higher test resolution under varying environment.
Further research needs to determine whether these can improve test precision.

This systematic review and meta-analysis comprehensively evaluated the accuracy and precision of VA assessments for both intertest and test-retest comparisons across four testing strategies, namely test site, optotype sampling, response input method, and level of supervision.

Our findings suggest that precision is more susceptible than accuracy to sources of variability, especially in remote and unsupervised testing, but this result needs to be solidified with more supporting studies.
With precision being consistent in between optotype sampling methods and response input methods reassure that these testing strategies might not be the main source of measurement variability.
Instead, future investigation and development should aim at development of VA charts with finer resolution and finding their association with precision.

While adaptive tests showed no meaningful difference than fixed-scale tests, their ability to sample smaller step size without compromising precision suggest their potential in detecting meaningful changes beyond measurement noise.
Hence, future VA development should utilize adaptive stimulus sampling and are recommended in clinical trials and for drug developments.

Test-retest accuracy (mean bias)
Rosser et al. found that changes of at least 0.20 logMAR could reliability distinguished from no change using the ETDRS chart(113).
More recently, Van der Zee et al. reported an overall mean random error of 0.20 logMAR across intertest and test-retest comparisons and proposed this values a provisional frame of reference(44).
Building on this work, our meta-analysis provides separate pooled estimates of intertest and testretest variability as each has distinct clinical implications.

Intertest variability addresses interchangeability between different tests, whereas test-retest variability helps distinguish true change in visual function from measurement error of the test itself when the same test was used repeatedly during longitudinal follow up.
The 0.19logMAR in overall intertest precision implied that switching tests can introduce substantial variation and even more pronounced with assessments conducted in non-clinical test sites.
These findings highlight the caution needed when integrating new VA tests into clinical practice or substituting them for established assessments.

Although eye care facilities often have established protocol for routine VA testing, maintaining consistent testing conditions is particularly important when these assessments are extended beyond professional eye care settings.

Examples include emergency departments, inpatient facilities and telehealth consultations, where rapid VA assessment is needed but testing environment may be difficult to standardize and testing instructions may be difficult to verify.
Additionally, the 0.14 logMAR in test-retest precision reflects that small changes on repeated testing may be difficult to distinguish from expected measurement variabilities.

Although the CoR of 0.14 logMAR fell within the 0.20 logMAR proposed by Rosser et al. and Van Der Zee et al., it remained greater than one ETDRS line (0.10 logMAR), suggesting that changes of this magnitude or smaller may still be obscured by measurement noise.
Further reduction in test-retest variability could improve sensitivity to subtle longitudinal changes in VA.
